\begin{abstract}
	Formal verification stalls from the cost of specification: to establish high-level facts, contracts have to be written for many supporting functions. Specification inference is one technique which can help by deriving specs from programs which can then be used to prove the primarily interesting properties. In this paper, we present a study for inference in the Move smart contract language, which has a specification language built in and strong verification support. We use an agent to run inference, and equip it with mechanical tools based on \emph{weakest precondition analysis}. Inference performance and quality is measured for three different inference tactics: pure agent inference, and two forms of hybrid inference with WP, while running against Opus~5, Sol~5.6, and Terra~5.6. As a corpus we use extracts from a real-world private product, avoiding bias from known code examples. The study shows multiple interesting results: first, pure model based spec inference works surprisingly well, tackling hard problems which require the agent to invent lemmas and helpers. Second, different models make different use of \WP: the mid-level model, Terra, benfits most by a 25\% reduction in API cost, whereas the higher end models do less. All have a lower error rate using \WP. In comparison, with help of \WP, Terra solves with the same success rate than the other models, but with much lower cost.
\end{abstract}

\Section{Per-Target Results}
\label{sec:appendix}

Tables~\ref{tab:opus}--\ref{tab:terra} give, for each target and arm, the mean cost per cell over the four replicates, mean input/output tokens in thousands (I/O k), the hybrid mean cost as a percentage of agent-only (vs. agent), and whether the specification succeeded at the first attempt and killed every held-out mutant (\Checkmark) or failed (\XSolidBrush, subscripted with the count where more than one replicate failed); $\ast$ marks cells whose scoring is still in progress and $\circ$ a cell lost to infrastructure.
All figures count up to the end of the first attempt; input counts include uncached, cached, and cache-creation tokens.
